description: Learn from the past, protect the future! In 1969, Apollo 12's landing sandblasted the Surveyor 3 probe with lunar dust. We tell its story for kids aged 10-14 and build a Monte Carlo simulation in Python that calculates how far future landers must stay from Moon bases and historic sites. We love physics, statistics and storytelling. Looking for: illustrators/designers, frontend devs (JavaScript, charts, animation) and anyone into space history or fact-checking. Join us!
summary:
In 1969, Apollo 12 landed about 155 m from the robotic lander Surveyor 3. The rocket plume sandblasted it with lunar dust, and the parts the astronauts brought home still carry the pits. Monte Carlo Moon turns this real incident into an interactive web app for school-age space fans and a tool for planning future landings.

Kids follow Surveyor 3's story in short scenes, then try it themselves: pick a lander, move the landing site and watch the dust cloud reach the hardware. Behind the story is our own Monte Carlo plume-surface interaction model in Python. It simulates regolith particles thrown up by the engine, compares 36 physics variants and keeps the ones that reproduce the impact pits measured on the returned Surveyor parts.

From those, the app computes how far a lander must stay from historic sites and future Moon bases. At Apollo-class thrust the median safe distance is roughly 3 km; a 30 m landing pad shrinks it to under 100 m. As Artemis and commercial landers return to the Moon, this matters: learn from the past, protect the future.
details:
What it does:

Monte Carlo Moon is a web app with three layers:

- Story mode (ages ~10–14): Surveyor 3 tells its own story in scenes – landing in 1967, the long lunar night, the Apollo 12 dust storm in 1969, the astronauts' visit and the lab analysis of its returned parts on Earth.

- Nerd mode (curious users and judges): the formulas, an interactive dust simulation with sliders for distance and engine thrust, damage maps, and the uncertainty of every result.

- Future planner: choose a historic site or a future Moon base and a lander size; the app shows the rings where the expected dust exposure drops below 1×, 0.1× and 0.01× of what hit Surveyor 3, including the effect of landing pads and berms. A 3D Moon globe and a heritage gallery of other NASA hardware left on the Moon, Mars and beyond tie it to the challenge theme.

How it works

- A plume-surface interaction model in Python (`psi_simulation.py`) follows the lander's descent, computes the plume's shear on the regolith, lifts particles from a lunar size distribution and flies them on ballistic paths in lunar gravity (no air drag, escape above ~2.38 km/s).

- Because the physics of plume erosion is uncertain, we do not trust a single model: we run 36 variants (3 published erosion laws × 2 velocity models × 6 ejection angles measured from Apollo landing films).

- Validation against real data: each variant is calibrated on the impact pits counted on Surveyor 3 parts returned by Apollo 12 (103 pits/cm² at 155 m). Only those that reproduce the measurement are kept.

- From those we compute, for each lander, the distance where exposure drops below a threshold, and report median, minimum and maximum across variants instead of one number.

- Additional studies: thrust escalation from 3.6 kN (Nova-C class) to 100 kN, repeated landings at the same site, and mitigation (landing pads of 10 m / 30 m radius, berms).

- The simulation writes one JSON file (`app_data.json`); the app builds all charts and sliders from it, so the model can improve without changing the app.

Key results (model, Apollo LM hover thrust 11.6 kN)

- Exposure equal to Surveyor 3's: median ≈ 330 m from the landing site.

- One tenth of Surveyor 3's exposure: median ≈ 3 km, with a range from ≈ 550 m to beyond 10 km across the plausible variants.

- A 30 m radius landing pad cuts the median 0.1× distance from ≈ 3 km to ≈ 60 m.

Benefits and intended impact

- Makes a real piece of NASA history tangible for children and shows that math and physics answer real questions.

- Gives mission planners, heritage advocates and students a transparent, data-anchored estimate of keep-out distances around historic sites (Apollo, Surveyor, Luna) and future Artemis-era bases.

- Shows the uncertainty honestly instead of hiding it in a single number.

Tools

Python, NumPy, SciPy, Numba (simulation and studies), HTML/CSS/JavaScript, three.js (3D Moon and landing scenes), NASA imagery and the NASA SVS CGI Moon Kit.

Creativity

Existing plume-erosion research is written for specialists. We combine a child-friendly story told by the spacecraft itself with a research-grade model that kids can play with, and with a "nerd mode" that exposes every formula and assumption.

Factors we considered

Scientific accuracy (every number traces back to a cited source), honest uncertainty, age-appropriate language, caveats on contested stories (e.g. the bacteria found in Surveyor's camera are today thought to be contamination on Earth), and that the app runs in any browser without installation.
